summary: Somalia lies in the Horn of Africa and has the longest coastline on the African continent; since the collapse of the central government in 1991 it has long been in a state of civil war and reconstruction.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: From the 7th century, Arab and Persian merchants came along the monsoon routes of the Red Sea and Indian Ocean to ports such as Zeila, Berbera and Mogadishu, and Islam arrived in the coastal cities with trade, adopting the Shafi'i school common in East Africa and Yemen. In the 19th century Sufi orders such as the Qadiriyya and Salihiyya penetrated the nomadic clans of the interior, making Islam a common identity that transcends clan divisions; in 1899–1920 Mohammed Abdullah Hassan even used religion to call for resistance against Britain and Italy. Because society is made up almost entirely of one people and one faith, the proportion of Muslims is close to the whole population.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: Christianity was introduced mainly by Catholic missionaries when Italy colonized the south in the late 19th century, and in 1928 the colonial government built a cathedral in Mogadishu, but the believers were mostly Italians and a few converts. In 1989 the Bishop of Mogadishu, Salvatore Colombo, was assassinated, the cathedral was destroyed after civil war broke out, and armed groups such as al-Shabaab regard conversion as apostasy and persecute converts, so very few Christians remain, mostly able to practice only in secret.

ranking.name: Others
ranking.description: This includes the faiths of a small number of foreign residents, and non-religious people who do not wish to declare themselves publicly. Somali society regards Islam as part of national identity, and abandoning Islam may bring rejection by one's family or even pursuit by armed groups, so people of other faiths and the non-religious can hardly declare themselves openly, and their actual numbers cannot be accurately counted.

religion.background: Islam arrived on the Somali coast through Red Sea and Indian Ocean trade in the 7th century, with Zeila and Mogadishu becoming early Islamic cities, and from the 13th century both the Mogadishu Sultanate and the Adal Sultanate were based on Islam. In the 19th century the Sufi orders spread the faith to the nomadic clans of the interior, and Islam became a common bond uniting the various clans. After the collapse of the central government in 1991, the Islamic Courts Union and later al-Shabaab tried to establish regimes based on religion, and religion thus also became caught up in the long-running civil war.

language.official: Somali and Arabic are the official languages.

ranking.name: Somali
ranking.description: Somali belongs to the Cushitic branch of the Afroasiatic family and is the mother tongue of the Somali people; the 'Maxaa' dialect used in the north and center forms the standard language, while the Digil and Rahanweyn clans of the south speak the very different 'Maay'. In 1972 the Siad Barre government adopted the Latin alphabet as the official script, and then in 1973–1975 launched a nationwide literacy campaign, making Somali the language of administration and education. Because the country is almost a single ethnic group, Somali naturally became the first language of the great majority.

ranking.name: Arabic
ranking.description: Arabic came with Islam and for hundreds of years has been the language of Quranic schools and religious scholars, and coastal merchants also know it through trade with the Arabian Peninsula. Somalia joined the Arab League in 1974, and the current constitution also makes Arabic co-official with Somali, but only a minority have it as their mother tongue, and most learn it only in religious settings or at school.

language.history: Somali belongs to the Cushitic branch, and for a long time oral poetry was its main literary form, with poets and poetry holding an exalted place in clan politics. In the 1920s Osman Yusuf Kenadid created the Osmanya script, but it did not become widespread; in 1972 the government formally adopted the Latin alphabet and promoted writing through a large-scale literacy campaign. During the colonial period the north was ruled by Britain and the south by Italy, English and Italian were administrative languages, and quite a few loanwords remain to this day. After the civil war of 1991, large numbers of refugees dispersed around the world, forming an important overseas Somali-speaking community.

ranking.name: Canjeero (Somali pancake)
ranking.description: A batter of sorghum, wheat or corn flour is fermented and then fried on a griddle into a thin pancake covered with air holes on the surface, with a slightly sour, soft texture. For breakfast it is often spread with ghee and sprinkled with sugar to go with tea, or eaten with stew.
ranking.history: Canjeero belongs to the same family as Ethiopia's injera and Yemen's lahoh, reflecting thousands of years of contact between the Horn of Africa and the Arabian Peninsula across the Red Sea. Sorghum is a drought-tolerant traditional crop of the Horn of Africa, and a fermented batter needs no oven, suiting nomadic and semi-nomadic families who cook it on a griddle. In Djibouti and Somaliland it is also called 'laxoox', and it remains the most common family breakfast, often appearing on the iftar table during Ramadan.

ranking.name: Bariis (Somali spiced rice)
ranking.description: Rice is cooked with a 'xawaash' spice powder mixing cumin, cardamom, cinnamon and cloves, often served with lamb or camel meat, with a banana on the side to eat with it.
ranking.history: Somalia itself produces little rice, and rice and spices were mainly imported from India and Arabia through the monsoon trade of the Indian Ocean; ports of the Benadir coast such as Mogadishu have been in contact with these regions since the Middle Ages, so spiced rice has a clear Indian and Arab flavor. Somalia has one of the largest herds of camels in the world, and camel meat with rice is a symbol of nomadic culture. Eating rice by hand and accompanying it with a banana is a distinctive Somali habit, and this dish is always on the table at weddings and Eid al-Fitr feasts.

ranking.name: Sambusa (triangular fried pastry)
ranking.description: Dough wrappers are filled with spiced minced beef or lamb, onion and chili, folded into triangles and deep-fried, with a crisp shell and a fragrant, spicy filling.
ranking.history: Sambusa derives from the 'sambusa' of Central Asia and the Middle East, which spread to India with Muslim merchants in the Middle Ages and then along the Indian Ocean trade network to the East African coast, with similar names everywhere. Indian migrants who came to do business in East Africa during the colonial period of the 19th and 20th centuries further popularized this snack. In Somalia it is the most common food for breaking the fast at sunset during Ramadan; households make large quantities in advance and freeze them, and it is also a small bite for entertaining guests at weddings and festivals.

ranking.name: Xalwo (Somali halwa)
ranking.description: Sugar, cornstarch, ghee and spices such as cardamom and nutmeg are cooked and stirred for a long time, and after cooling become a glossy, chewy sweet similar to a soft candy.
ranking.history: The word 'halwa' comes from the Arabic for 'sweet'; in the Middle East and South Asia it is mostly made with tahini or semolina, while the Somali version is cooked from starch and sugar into a gel, in a class of its own. Traditionally it requires hours of constant stirring and so is mostly made by specialist makers and is regarded as a precious sweet for guests. At Somali weddings, Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha, xalwo is always served with coffee or milky tea, and overseas Somali communities also regard it as representative of the taste of home.

ranking.name: Shaah (Somali spiced milk tea)
ranking.description: Black tea is boiled with spices such as cardamom, cinnamon and cloves, then plenty of sugar and milk or camel milk are added, with a sweet, rich flavor.
ranking.history: The word 'shaah' shares its origin with the Arabic and Persian words for 'tea'; tea spread through Indian Ocean trade and through the British colonial network in Somaliland in the late 19th century, while the spiced way of brewing was influenced by India and Arabia. Somalis drink tea several times a day, and street tea houses are places for men to gather, exchange news, discuss politics and recite poetry. Serving spiced milk tea to guests is basic courtesy, and at teatime it is often accompanied by sambusa or small snacks.
